meta.blurb: A plague strikes Athens, a city packed with people who fled the enemy army, and one of the sick writes down all he sees. Thucydides records most of a long war with Sparta, from great speeches to a doomed fleet at Syracuse.
meta.bible: Thucydides: an Athenian, born around 460 BC, general in 424 BC, exiled for twenty years after failing to save Amphipolis, author of this unfinished history, which stops in the year 411 BC in mid-sentence. He caught the plague and survived. The war: the Peloponnesian War between Athens (with its empire) and Sparta (with its allies), 431 to 404 BC; Thucydides calls it greater than any earlier war. Athens: democracy, sea power, ships called Triremes, the port of Piraeus joined to the city by the Long Walls, an empire of allies who paid tribute. Sparta: an army of Hoplites, citizens trained for war, ruled by two kings and a council of Ephors, its land worked by Helots. Pericles: Athens's leading general and speaker, plan: never fight the Spartans on land and trust the fleet; gave the Funeral Oration in the winter of 431 to 430 BC; died of plague in 429 BC. Archidamus: king of Sparta who warned against war and then led the first invasions of Attica. Sthenelaidas: the Spartan Ephor who called for the vote. Cleon: loud Athenian leader, pushed for harsh punishment of Mytilene, captured the Spartans at Pylos, killed at Amphipolis in 422 BC. Diodotus: argued for mercy for Mytilene. Demosthenes: Athenian general who fortified Pylos and later led the reinforcements to Sicily; executed after Syracuse. Nicias: cautious, rich and sick Athenian general; made the peace of 421 BC and led the Sicilian expedition; executed after Syracuse. Brasidas: bold Spartan general who took Amphipolis in 424 BC and was killed there in 422 BC. Alcibiades: brilliant, rich, ambitious young Athenian; pushed for Sicily; recalled in 415 BC, fled to Sparta. Lamachus: third general in Sicily, killed in 414 BC. Gylippus: Spartan commander who saved Syracuse. Lysander: Spartan admiral who won in 405 BC. Places and events: Corinth, Corcyra (now Corfu), Epidamnus, Potidaea, Attica (the land of Athens), Plataea (besieged 429 to 427 BC), Mytilene on Lesbos (revolt 428 BC), Pylos and Sphacteria (425 BC), Amphipolis, Melos (416 BC), Sicily and Syracuse (415 to 413 BC), the river Assinarus, Aegospotami (405 BC), the Persian king. Dates are BC, so the numbers fall as time passes, and approximate numbers are marked as about. The Melian Dialogue and the speeches are Thucydides's own versions of what was said, as he tells us. Voice and tone: serious, clear and fair, as if told by a careful witness; violence is stated plainly with no gore; each beat names the part of the History it comes from.

B1B2: Thucydides was an Athenian who began to write the history of a war between Athens and Sparta as soon as it started. He felt sure that it would be the greatest war the Greeks had ever known.
Thucydides did not want to write an entertaining story. He wanted to write something useful for ever, so he checked every report carefully, and he asked many witnesses what they had seen.
In the first part of Book 1, Thucydides looks back at early Greece. He shows that the towns were small and poor and seldom acted together, so earlier wars were much smaller than this one.

Athens was a rich sea power, and its people voted on important matters in a public meeting. Sparta was a land power with the finest soldiers in Greece, and its citizens trained for war all their lives.
After the Persian wars, Athens led a league of allies who paid money to keep a fleet. Over time the league became an empire, because Athens did not let cities leave.
A quarrel began at Epidamnus, a city on the coast far from Athens, and it involved Corcyra and Corinth. Corcyra asked Athens for help, and Athens sent ships to join the fight against Corinth.
Corinth urged Sparta to act, because Athens was besieging Potidaea, a city that Corinth had founded. Other cities also complained about Athens, and a meeting was held to decide whether to go to war.
King Archidamus warned the Spartans that war with Athens would be long and hard. But another leader, Sthenelaidas, called for a vote, and most Spartans shouted that Athens had broken the peace.
Thucydides says that Corinth and Corcyra were only the stated reasons for the war. The real cause was the growth of Athenian power, which made Sparta afraid.
Pericles, the leader of Athens, had a clear plan for the war. He wanted the Athenians to stay behind their walls, avoid land battles, and use the fleet and the empire's money.
In the summer of 431 BC the Spartans marched into Attica and burned the farmland. The farmers had moved inside the walls of Athens, and they were angry to watch their homes burn.
After the first year of fighting, Pericles gave a speech to honour the dead. In Book 2, Thucydides gives it as a great praise of Athens and its democracy, where power is in the hands of the many.

Pericles told the crowd to look at the greatness of Athens each day until they loved it. The fallen soldiers had died for this city, and he said that famous people have the whole earth as their grave.
In the second summer of the war, a terrible plague began in Athens. The city was crowded with country people, and the sickness spread quickly through the narrow streets and the hot houses.
Thucydides had the plague himself and survived, so he describes it with care. Many people died, and with death all around them, some stopped obeying the law and others stopped praying.
The suffering made the Athenians blame Pericles, and they punished him with a fine. Soon they chose him as their general again, but he died of the plague in 429 BC.
Plataea was a small city that was loyal to Athens. The Spartans and their allies surrounded it for a long time, and at last it fell in 427 BC.
In 428 BC the island city of Mytilene rebelled against Athens. Athens sent a fleet, and after a siege, the city was forced to give up.
The assembly first voted to kill every man in Mytilene. The next day they had doubts, and in the debate that followed, Cleon asked for harsh punishment, but Diodotus argued that mercy would be wiser.
A ship had already left with the first order, so a second ship sailed after it with the new one. The crew rowed day and night and arrived just in time to save the city.
In Corcyra the poor and the rich fought each other in a civil war, and many were killed. Thucydides says that during such struggles people changed the meaning of words to suit their actions.
In 425 BC the Athenian general Demosthenes built a rough fort at Pylos, on the coast of the Spartan lands. The Spartans were alarmed and rushed to attack it by land and sea.

The Athenian fleet beat the Spartan ships and trapped about four hundred Spartan soldiers on the island of Sphacteria. Sparta asked for peace, but Cleon refused and promised to take the men in twenty days.
Cleon and Demosthenes attacked the island and made the Spartans surrender. Everyone had believed that Spartans would die before they gave up, so this news surprised all the Greeks.
In 424 BC the bold Spartan Brasidas marched north and made Amphipolis surrender. Thucydides, who led ships nearby, arrived that same evening, but he was too late to save the city.
The Athenians blamed Thucydides for the loss of Amphipolis and sent him away from his city for twenty years. As an exile he could meet people from both sides, and he kept writing his history.
In 422 BC Cleon led an army to take back Amphipolis, and there Brasidas defeated him. Both leaders died in the battle, and both had been strong enemies of peace.

In 421 BC Nicias, a careful and wealthy Athenian general, helped to make a peace with Sparta that was meant to last for fifty years. But neither side kept all its promises, and the peace soon began to fail.
A new leader named Alcibiades appeared in Athens after the peace was made. He was young, rich, clever and very ambitious, and he pushed the city toward bold actions against Sparta.
In 416 BC the Athenians sent ships and soldiers to Melos, a small island that wished to stay neutral. The leaders of Melos were invited to talk, but they were not allowed to speak to the whole city.
The Athenians said that talk of justice only matters between equals. They believed that the strong do what they can and the weak accept what they must, but the Melians still trusted in the gods.
Melos refused to surrender, and Sparta did not come to help. After a siege, the Athenians took the island, killed the men and sold the women and children.
Envoys came from Segesta, a city in Sicily, and asked Athens for help against its enemy Selinus. They promised money, and the Athenians began to dream of conquering the great island.
Nicias warned the assembly that a war in Sicily would be too big and too far away. Alcibiades spoke boldly in reply, and the assembly voted to send a very large fleet.
In summer 415 BC the fleet sailed from the port of Piraeus. The whole city came to see it, and they prayed and sang as the ships left.
Just before the fleet sailed, someone broke many of the stone statues of Hermes in Athens. Alcibiades was accused, called back from Sicily, and instead of going home he escaped to Sparta.
In Sicily the Athenians besieged Syracuse, the biggest city on the island, by building a wall around it. The general Lamachus was killed, and Nicias, who was often ill, was left in sole command.
Sparta sent a commander named Gylippus to help Syracuse, as Alcibiades had advised. He arrived in time, and the Athenians failed to finish their wall.
Nicias wrote a long letter to Athens, describing how his army was tired and ill. He asked to be recalled or reinforced, and the Athenians sent Demosthenes with a second fleet.
Demosthenes led a night attack on the high ground above Syracuse. In the dark, the Athenians could not tell friends from enemies, and they were beaten with heavy losses.
Demosthenes wanted to leave Sicily at once, and Nicias finally agreed. But then there was an eclipse of the moon, and the priests said that they should wait nearly a month.
The Syracusans closed the mouth of their harbour and trapped the Athenian ships inside. In the last sea battle, with the shore crowded with watching soldiers, the Athenians were beaten.
The Athenian army left on foot, with the wounded and the sick. The enemy attacked them all the way, and at the river Assinarus, thirsty men rushed into the water and were killed.
About seven thousand prisoners were kept in the stone quarries of Syracuse, where they suffered from hunger, thirst, heat and cold. Many died, and the Syracusans put Nicias and Demosthenes to death.
When news of the disaster reached Athens, at first nobody believed it. Then the people were angry and afraid, but they decided to build new ships and fight on.
In 411 BC a small group of rich Athenians took power and ended the democracy. The fleet at Samos stayed loyal to democracy, and after about four months the group lost control.
Book 8 of Thucydides ends suddenly in the middle of a sentence in the year 411 BC. No one knows exactly why he stopped writing, but it was probably because he died.

Other writers tell us the rest of the story, which Thucydides never lived to write. In 405 BC the Spartan admiral Lysander destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami, and Athens, starved by a blockade, gave up in 404 BC.
Thucydides seems to have returned to Athens after the war ended. He died around 400 BC, but his unfinished book has been read by students, soldiers and leaders for more than two thousand years.
Thucydides shows that fear, pride and self-interest push nations toward war. He also shows how war can change people, so that the same mistakes can be made again.
C1C2: In 431 BC a quarrel between the two strongest powers in Greece turned into open war, and an Athenian named Thucydides began to write it down from the very first day. He believed, correctly as it turned out, that it would be the greatest upheaval the Greek world had ever seen. His History, begun in that spirit of alarm, was never quite finished, and the story of how it was written is almost as remarkable as the story it tells.

Thucydides says plainly, at the start of Book 1, that his History is not meant as a prize entry for a single evening's applause, but as a possession for all time. He recorded what he had seen himself or what he had learned from eyewitnesses, whose accounts he cross-examined with painstaking suspicion. He hoped that anyone who wished to understand the future, which in human affairs usually resembles the past, would find clear and honest guidance in his pages.

In the opening chapters of Book 1, Thucydides surveys the distant past and argues that early Greece was a land of scattered, insecure and poorly organised communities, whose wars had been small affairs. Even the famous expedition against Troy, he suggests, was less impressive than the poets liked to make it seem. Only in his own lifetime, he insists, had the resources of money, ships and men grown great enough to make a truly enormous war possible.

Athens was a daring, restless city with a powerful fleet, whose citizens voted on great matters in a public assembly and prided themselves on speed of action. Sparta, by contrast, was a slow and cautious land power, ruled by two kings and a small council, whose citizens were trained for war from childhood and who relied on the labour of enslaved Helots. Thucydides saw that each of them was strong exactly where the other was weak, and this made the conflict long and hard to settle.

After the Greek victories over Persia, Athens became the leader of a league of cities that paid money into a common fund for the fleet. In the years that followed, the league turned little by little into an empire, because Athens collected the money, commanded the ships, and punished any city that tried to withdraw. Many of the subjects resented this, and when war came, they were ready to welcome any power that might set them free.

The trouble began at Epidamnus, a distant coastal city, where a local quarrel drew in the island of Corcyra and its powerful mother city, Corinth. When Corcyra, which had a large fleet, sought an alliance with Athens, the Athenians agreed to a defensive pact, partly because they did not wish the Corcyran ships to fall into Corinthian hands. Corinth was furious, and it began to seek revenge by stirring up the allies of Sparta against the Athenians.

Corinth had a second grievance, for Potidaea, a city that it had founded, had revolted against Athens, and the Athenians were besieging it. The Corinthians travelled to Sparta, where they accused the Spartans of sleeping while Athens grew stronger every year. Other allies spoke of their own complaints, and the Spartan assembly was called upon to decide whether Athens had broken the peace.

The wise old King Archidamus warned his countrymen that Athens was wealthy, experienced and difficult to attack, and that the war would be handed down as a burden to their children. Yet an official named Sthenelaidas answered with a short, blunt speech and put the matter to the vote by having the citizens shout, and the louder shout was for war. Thucydides notes that the Spartans were moved less by the arguments of their allies than by their fear of Athens's growing power.

Thucydides draws a sharp line between the quarrels that people spoke of and the cause that lay beneath them. The complaints about Corcyra, Potidaea and trade, he says, were only the open grievances, whereas the truest cause, though the least often mentioned, was the growth of Athens and the fear it aroused in Sparta. That one sentence has been quoted by readers ever since, because it seems to describe how many great powers have drifted into war.

Pericles, who was the most influential figure in Athens, proposed a plan that depended on patience and on the city's special strengths. He urged his fellow citizens never to meet the Spartan army in the open field, but to retreat behind their walls, to rely on their fleet and wealth, and to wait until their enemy grew tired. Thucydides admires the plan, and he says that Athens might well have won if it had been followed.

In the summer of 431 BC the Spartan army, led by King Archidamus, marched into Attica and began to burn crops and farmhouses within sight of Athens. The country people, who had crowded behind the walls on Pericles's advice, watched the smoke with growing rage and demanded that the army march out to fight. Pericles refused to be pushed, and he sent the fleet out to raid the coast of the Peloponnese in reply.

At the public funeral held after the first year of the war, Pericles delivered the speech that Thucydides reports in Book 2, though in words that are probably his own version of the argument. He praised Athens as a democracy in which power rested with the many rather than the few, where talent counted for more than rank, and where citizens enjoyed freedom in their private lives. The city, he declared, was a lesson to all of Greece, and the men who had died had given their lives for its sake.

Pericles urged the mourners to fix their eyes on the power of their city every day, until they became its lovers, and to remember that its greatness had been won by brave men who knew their duty. The dead, he said, had given up their lives for it, and they would never be forgotten, for famous men have the whole earth as their tomb. He ended with a gentle appeal to the grieving parents, and with a promise that the city would support the children of the fallen.

In the second year of the war a terrible plague broke out in Athens, which was packed with refugees from the countryside living in huts and in the stifling heat. It had apparently begun far to the south and arrived through the harbour at Piraeus, and neither doctors nor priests could do anything about it. Thucydides tells us that nothing like it had been remembered, and he describes it in detail so that readers might recognise it if it should ever come again.

Thucydides, who suffered from the plague himself and recovered, describes its symptoms with the cool precision of an observer who wishes his account to be useful. Doctors died first because they were closest to the sick, prayers and oracles proved useless, and the number of the dead grew so large that the bodies were piled in the temples. Faced with such disaster, many Athenians gave up their respect for law and religion and decided to enjoy themselves while they still could.

As the suffering continued, the Athenians turned against Pericles, took away his command and fined him, even though they had followed his plan faithfully. Before long they changed their minds and elected him general once more, but the plague caught him as well, and he died in the autumn of 429 BC. Thucydides thinks that the city never again found so steady a leader, and he complains that those who followed him let ambition and quarrels spoil his careful strategy.

The little city of Plataea, which had long been a friend of Athens, was surrounded in 429 BC by a Spartan army that built a siege wall and piled up earth against the defences. After a brave defence, some of the people slipped out over the wall on a stormy winter night, but those who remained had to surrender in 427 BC. Most of the captured defenders were put to death, the city was destroyed, and Thucydides records the whole sad story with unusual care.

In 428 BC Mytilene, the chief city of the island of Lesbos, rebelled against Athens and sent envoys to Sparta to beg for help. The Spartans were slow to act, and the Athenians dispatched a fleet, besieged the city and compelled it to surrender in the following year. The question of how to punish the rebels now landed before the Athenian assembly, where it was to be decided in a famous debate.

In the first debate the assembly, urged on by the forceful Cleon, voted to put to death every grown man in Mytilene and to enslave the women and children. By the next morning, however, many citizens were horrified at their own cruelty, and the assembly met again, where Diodotus argued that harsh punishment would not stop revolts and that mercy was simply better for Athens. The vote that followed was extremely close, and in the end mercy won by only a small margin of hands.

A ship carrying the cruel first decree had already sailed a full day earlier, and so the Athenians sent off a second ship to overtake it. The oarsmen rowed through the night, eating and sleeping in turns, and they reached Mytilene just as the general there was reading out the first order. Even so, the Athenians executed a little over a thousand of those most responsible for the rebellion, and the city's walls were torn down.

In Corcyra the party of the people and the party of the rich turned against each other in a savage civil war, each calling on one side of the great struggle for help. Thucydides observes that in such times words changed their meaning, so that reckless daring was called courage and careful thought was called cowardice. He shows how war could poison a society from inside, and the passage remains among the most quoted in his book.

In 425 BC an Athenian fleet sailing around the Peloponnese landed at Pylos, where the general Demosthenes persuaded his men to throw up a hasty fortification on the rocky headland. Sparta, startled to find an enemy base within its own lands, withdrew its army from Attica and hurried to retake the place by sea and land. Their attack failed, however, and in the confusion that followed, something happened that no one in Greece had thought possible.

The Athenian navy defeated the Spartan fleet and stranded a force of about four hundred soldiers on the island of Sphacteria, among them many of the best-born Spartans. The anxious Spartans asked for peace, but Cleon persuaded the assembly to demand more than they would give, and then, when the siege dragged on, rashly promised to bring the men home within twenty days. He was mocked for the boast, but he took up the challenge and sailed out to Pylos with fresh troops.

Demosthenes and Cleon landed on the island with archers and light troops, who attacked the Spartans from every side, and after a hard day the exhausted survivors, nearly three hundred men, laid down their arms. Greeks everywhere had believed that a Spartan would die rather than surrender, and the news struck them like thunder. The prisoners were held in Athens as hostages, and Sparta was left afraid to invade Attica again.

In the winter of 424 BC the Spartan commander Brasidas, a general of rare daring and persuasive tongue, led an army across northern Greece and offered the city of Amphipolis such mild terms that it surrendered at once. Thucydides, who was in command of a squadron nearby, sailed to help, and he arrived the same evening, only to find the city already lost. He managed to save the port of Eion, but he could not undo the damage.

The Athenians held Thucydides responsible for the loss of Amphipolis, and they condemned him to twenty years of exile from his native city. It was a bitter blow, but he notes that exile gave him the chance to see events from both sides of the conflict and to question men on every side. That unusual freedom may be part of the reason that his History is so fair, calm and resistant to patriotic bias.

In 422 BC Cleon led an Athenian army north to recover Amphipolis, but Brasidas struck him while his men were retreating, and the Athenians were routed. Cleon was killed as he fled, and Brasidas died of his wounds soon afterwards, and the city honoured him as a hero. Thucydides remarks that the two men who had been most opposed to peace were now gone, and that the way was open for the leaders who wanted it.

In 421 BC the cautious and wealthy Athenian general Nicias helped to negotiate a treaty with Sparta that was intended to last for fifty years. It was a flawed document, since neither side surrendered all that it had promised, and several important Spartan allies refused to accept it. Thucydides insists that the war should be regarded as a single twenty-seven-year struggle, because this so-called peace was merely a pause full of mistrust and little battles.

A new figure now came to the front in Athens, the young and dazzling Alcibiades, who was rich, handsome, clever and quite unashamed of his own ambition. He urged the city to break the fragile peace and to seek new alliances against Sparta, partly because he believed that such a course would make his own name immortal. His admirers loved his boldness, while his enemies feared that his love of display and power would one day bring disaster.

In 416 BC an Athenian force arrived at Melos, a small island that had refused to join the Athenian empire and wished to be left in peace. Before attacking, the Athenian commanders asked to speak with the island's leaders in private, and Thucydides reports their conversation in what is known as the Melian Dialogue. He admits openly that he has reconstructed the speeches, but the general sense, he says, is accurate.

The Athenian envoys declared that questions of right and wrong carry weight only between equals, and that in the real world the strong do what they can while the weak suffer what they must. The Melians replied that they trusted the gods and the Spartans to help them, and that submitting at once would be a kind of death. The Athenians called such hopes foolish, and they warned the Melians that Sparta seldom risked its own people for the sake of others.

The Melians chose to resist, and the Athenians besieged the island, while the Spartans, as the Athenians had predicted, sent no help. In the winter the town was betrayed from within and surrendered, and the victors killed the grown men and sold the women and children into slavery. Thucydides records the fate of Melos without comment, and readers have ever since felt the force of his silence.

In 415 BC envoys arrived from Segesta in Sicily to plead for Athenian help against a neighbouring city, and they promised that their treasury would pay for a large expedition. The Athenians, who knew little about the size or strength of the island, found the idea of expanding their empire westward irresistible. Thucydides says that most citizens had only a vague notion of how big Sicily was, and that the whole adventure grew from ambition more than from need.

Nicias spoke against the expedition, warning that Sicily was large, far away and filled with cities as strong as Athens, and that the city would be foolish to start a new war before finishing the old one. Alcibiades answered with youthful confidence, promising glory and wealth, and the excited crowd was swept along. When Nicias tried to frighten them by naming a huge number of ships and men, the assembly simply voted for everything he had asked.

In the summer of 415 BC the expedition sailed from Piraeus in the most splendid display that Athens had ever offered, with more than a hundred warships and many transports. A huge crowd gathered along the shore to pray, to sing hymns and to watch their sons, brothers and friends depart under three generals, Nicias, Alcibiades and Lamachus. Thucydides says that the sight was so grand that people could scarcely believe it, and later events made it seem unbearably sad.

Shortly before the fleet sailed, almost all the stone statues of the god Hermes in Athens were mutilated in a single night, an act that was seen as a terrible religious crime and a sign of conspiracy. Alcibiades, who had enemies, was accused of this and of mocking sacred rites, and when he was summoned home from Sicily to stand trial he slipped away and fled to Sparta. Athens condemned him to death in his absence, and the man who had pushed for the campaign soon became its worst enemy.

In Sicily the Athenians began a siege of Syracuse, the strongest Greek city on the island, and tried to cut it off by building a great wall across the hills that surrounded it. The brave general Lamachus fell in a skirmish, and Nicias, a sick and anxious man, was left alone in command of the whole army. The Syracusans, who had been close to despair, took heart as the Athenians' energy began to fade.

Alcibiades had advised Sparta to send a commander to Syracuse, and the Spartans chose Gylippus, who slipped across the sea and reached the city just as the Syracusans were about to give up. He took charge of the defence, built a counter-wall across the Athenian line, and brought up fresh allies from other parts of the island. The besiegers, who had been about to win, were suddenly the besieged, and the tide was turning.

Nicias wrote a long and honest letter to the Athenian assembly, describing how his ships were rotting, his men were deserting and the enemy cavalry was growing stronger. He asked either to be replaced because of his illness or to be given large reinforcements, and the Athenians, unwilling to admit failure, chose the second course. They sent out Demosthenes, the hero of Pylos, with a second great fleet and thousands of fresh soldiers.

Demosthenes decided on a bold stroke, a night attack on the heights above Syracuse, hoping to surprise the enemy and finish the war quickly. At first it went well, but in the darkness and confusion the Athenians lost their way, mistook friends for foes, and fell into panic as the defenders came at them. Many were killed or fell from the cliffs, and Thucydides remarks that no one could say with certainty what had happened in that night battle.

Demosthenes argued that the army should leave Sicily at once, and Nicias, after much hesitation, finally agreed to prepare the ships. Then, in August 413 BC, the moon was eclipsed, and Nicias, who was very devout, took the advice of the soothsayers and put off the departure for twenty-seven days. Thucydides says that this superstition was one cause of the disaster, for in those weeks the Syracusans closed all the ways out.

The Syracusans blocked the mouth of the Great Harbour with ships and chains, and the Athenians were obliged to fight their way out in a desperate battle in the narrow water. The shores were crowded with both armies watching, and every wave of the fight was followed with cheers and groans, so that the noise was as great as the clash of the ships. When the Athenians were beaten, they lost both their fleet and their last hope of leaving by sea.

The Athenian army set off overland, with the sick and wounded begging not to be left behind, and for a week the enemy cavalry and archers harassed them at every step. At the river Assinarus, desperate with thirst, the men rushed into the water while the Syracusans shot at them from the bank, and the stream ran thick with mud and blood. Demosthenes had already surrendered with his part of the army, and Nicias soon surrendered his own to Gylippus.

About seven thousand prisoners were shut up in the deep stone quarries of Syracuse, where they suffered from the burning sun by day, the cold by night, and from hunger, thirst and disease. After about ten weeks the survivors were sold as slaves, and the Syracusans put Nicias and Demosthenes to death, although Gylippus had hoped to spare them. Thucydides says that this was the greatest event of the whole war, most glorious for the victors and most ruinous for the vanquished.

When the first news of the disaster reached Athens, the people refused to believe it, and when it was confirmed they turned on the speakers who had urged the expedition. Fear of a Spartan attack and of revolt among their allies then overwhelmed them, yet the Athenians resolved to build a new fleet, to save money and to keep fighting. Thucydides marvels that a city so battered could continue the war for so many more years.

In 411 BC a small group of wealthy conspirators, claiming that only a narrower government could win the war, seized power in Athens and set up a council of four hundred. The fleet at Samos, however, remained loyal to democracy and refused to accept the new rulers, and within a few months the oligarchs were driven out, replaced by a broader form of government. Thucydides, who had little sympathy for the extremes of either side, praised the moderate government that followed.

The eighth and last book of Thucydides breaks off suddenly in the middle of a sentence, in the autumn of the year 411 BC, with the war still undecided and almost seven years left to run. We cannot be sure why he stopped, but it seems likely that death interrupted him, though some scholars think he may simply have been unable to finish. The unfinished state of the book gives it a haunting quality, as if history itself had refused to end.

Writers who came later, such as Xenophon, completed the story that Thucydides left unfinished. In 405 BC the Spartan admiral Lysander destroyed the last Athenian fleet at Aegospotami, and a long blockade starved Athens into surrender in 404 BC, with the help of Persian money for Sparta. The long walls that had protected the city were pulled down to the music of flute players, and the democracy of Pericles was replaced for a time by a cruel government of thirty rulers.

According to ancient tradition, Thucydides returned to Athens when the war ended and the exiles were allowed to come home, and he died not long afterwards, around 400 BC, though the details of his death are uncertain. He left behind an unfinished masterpiece, which scholars, statesmen and soldiers have studied for more than two thousand years. Few ancient writers have been trusted so thoroughly for their honesty and their cool, clear-sighted view of men at war.

The History of Thucydides remains alive because it shows how fear, pride and the hunger for power can draw even clever peoples into disasters that they might have avoided. It shows democracies making brilliant and terrible decisions, and it shows how long wars wear down laws, language and human kindness. Thucydides wrote that human nature would not change, and so, he hoped, his account would serve as a guide for anyone who wished to see a clear picture of the past.
